extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, lawgivers, and readers of political philosophy and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Critical examination of principles for designing and judging constitutions and forms of government, focusing on balance of powers, accountability, election design, and popular capacity. The text compares simple democracies, mixed governments, hereditary and elective systems with historical examples and practical safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of power in a single authority
rubrics_metrics.description: An attempt, or suspicion of one, to grasp all power into the hands of the crown, had proved the destruction both of king and lords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutions to prevent the centralization of all authority in one person or body; beware that entangling constitutions with spiritual lords, elective lords, or decayed boroughs can enable such concentration and lead to tyranny and collapse (historical cautionary examples are cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: People must be sufficiently enlightened to choose governors
rubrics_metrics.description: If the people cannot be sufficiently enlightened, by education and the press, to despise and resent insults and impositions on human nature, all pretences of right ... they will be duped by them in one assembly more than in three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A functioning representative system presumes an informed electorate; public education and a free press are prerequisites for the people's capacity to choose governors wisely and to resist demagoguery and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government / balance of monarchy, aristocracy, democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: An equal mixture of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy, is the only free government which has been able to manage the greatest heroes and statesmen ... so as to keep them always obedient to the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a tripartite or balanced constitution (mixture of branches/classes) because each branch checks the others: the king and commons check lords, lords and commons check king, etc. This mixture prevents any one individual or group from becoming dominant and provides durable protection against usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent individuals from becoming 'over great' — preserve equability
rubrics_metrics.description: To assume the bare and title of nobility ... 'that no man be permitted to grow over great in power.' 'Nor any rank above the ordinary standard.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional provisions should limit accumulation of personal power, hereditary privileges, and ranks that produce unequal political influence. Mechanisms like rotation, ballots, and restrictions on titles and entailed power seek to maintain an 'equability of condition' to curb petty tyrants and prevent oligarchic or popular idolatries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability of officers and governors through periodic elections and legal liability
rubrics_metrics.description: In form all powers are accountable for misdemeanors in government, in regard of the nimble returns and periods of the people's election ... he that ere while was a governor, being reduced to the condition of a subject, lies open to the force of the laws, and may with ease be brought to punishment for his offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide frequent, regular electoral returns and legal mechanisms so that those who exercise power can be reduced to subject status and held legally responsible; ministers should be accountable for acts done in office and subject to enquiry and punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit standing, unaccountable powers and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: All 'standing powers' (meaning unlimited, unbalanced, standing powers, as hereditary simple monarchies and aristocracies) have and ever do assume unto themselves an arbitrary exercise of their own wills ... so that, though they commit all the injustice in the world, they are not bound to give an account of their action to any but to God himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid permanent, unaccountable institutions or offices that can entrench arbitrary dominion; constitutional design should ensure that powers are not settled in perpetuity without meaningful checks and contestability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards against venality, faction, bribery and corruption in elections
rubrics_metrics.description: This violent declamation ... does not remove the danger of venality, faction, sedition, and civil war, in the choice of governors and senators, principles more brutish and irrational ... than hereditary-kings and senates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt procedural devices (ballots, rotations, complex election contrivances) and anti-corruption measures to reduce bribery, vote-buying, manipulation by factions, and the undue influence of party machines during elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure/simple democracy that permits majority or popular tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: In a simple democracy no ballots or rotations can prevent it; one single tyrant will rule the whole commonwealth at his pleasure ... nothing to prevent him from employing the whole executive and judicial power, nothing to prevent him from applying the public purse to the augmentation of his own popularity and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple majoritarian systems, without institutional checks or separations, risk empowering a popular tyrant; constitutional structures should include balancing bodies and procedural limits to restrain majoritarian excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent incumbents and parties from entrenching by control of offices, judiciary, and public funds
rubrics_metrics.description: He that was once a governor, will generally continue always a governor, because he will apply all the executive and judicial authority, and even the public money ... to increase that party in the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design separation and accountability so incumbents cannot use state offices, judicial manipulation, or public funds to entrench their party or perpetuate themselves in power. Guard against clientelism and partisan capture of institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide lawful, institutional means to check tyrants rather than relying on assassination
rubrics_metrics.description: Killing one tyrant only makes way for a worse, unless the people have sense, spirit, and honesty enough to establish and support a constitution guarded at all points against tyranny; against the tyranny of the one, the few, and the many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should offer robust legal remedies and institutional checks to remove or sanction tyrannical actors; reliance on violent means (tyrannicide) is unstable and likely to produce worse outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design elective or hereditary executive arrangements mindful of historical pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations too have tried the experiment of elective monarchies ... but after long miseries, wars, and carnage, they have always determined chance to be better than choice, and hereditary princes preferable to elective ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical experience to inform whether elective executives or hereditary ones are more stable in a given context; electoral arrangements for high offices must be designed to avoid factional violence, instability, and repeated contests that produce war or decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep officers and governors questionable and removable by representative bodies where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In Switzerland the people are free indeed, because all officers and governors in the cantons are questionable by the people in their successive assemblies.' 'The English constitution ... all officers are questionable, and often have been questioned, by the people in their successive assemblies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate mechanisms (questioning, inquiry, parliamentary scrutiny, recall) that allow assemblies or the people to examine and remove officials; ensure practical procedures exist for bringing those in power to account without resorting to violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve popular morals and understanding to support constitutional safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Let it be the study, therefore, of law-givers and philosophers, to enlighten the people's understandings, and improve their morals, by good and general education; to enable them to comprehend the scheme of government, and to know upon what points their liberties depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design must be accompanied by civic education and moral improvement: educating citizens about governmental institutions, rights, and the points on which liberties depend is essential to prevent populist errors and support stable constitutional practice.
